card.profile_long: Shalako is a series of dances and ceremonies conducted by the Native American Zuni people for the Zuni people at the winter solstice, typically following the harvest. The Shalako ceremony and feast has been closed to non-native peoples since 1990, though non-native peoples may be invited as guests by a Zuni tribal member. Nancy Bonvillain described the Shalakos, noting that "They brought good fortune, abundant crops, and many children." They are chosen at Winter Solstice, when they begin to learn the chants they will recite in the early December ceremony. The mythology surrounding the ceremonies includes the Koyemshi, consisting of nine offspring and their father, Awan Tatchu, who accompany and interpret the kachinas. The children have characteristics of their father, dun-colored and marked with welts, including Awan Pekwin (Priest-speaker of the Sun), Awan Pithlashiwanni (Bow Priest-warrior), Eshotsi (the Bat), Itsepasha (the Glum or Aggrieved), Kalutsi (the Suckling), Tsathlashi (Old-youth), Muyapona (Wearer of the Eyelets of Invisibility), Posuki (the Pouter), and Nalashi (Aged Buck). The ceremony is preceded by the Council of the Gods. Shulawitsi, Little Fire God, and his father, Shulawatsi An Tatchu, precede the Shalako, with Shulawitsi portrayed by a young boy carrying cedar bark torches who lights preparatory fires. They are followed by Saiyatasha or Longhorn, Rain Priest of the North, and Hututu, Rain Priest of the South, accompanied by a Yamuhakto, their helpers. All are protected by the Salimopia, Warriors of the Six Directions, which include the Salimopia Shelow'ona from the south, Salimopia Kohan'ona from the east, Salimopia Thlian'ona from the west, Salimopia Thluptsin'ona from the north, Salimopia Shikan'ona from the nadir, and Salimopia Itapanahnan'ona from the zenith. Each kiva selects two men, one to portray one of the six Shalakos, and one who alternates in the role, the Shalako Anuthlona. They appear after the Council of the Gods complete their journey around the village at dusk. They approach the village from the south, coming down Greasy Hill. Each Shalako enters their designated house, and chants commence recounting the creation of the Zuni, and their search for the Middle. After midnight, a feast is consumed by all, followed with dancing by the Shalako. The ceremony finishes at dawn when Saiyatasha completes his final prayer.
card.sacred_note: The Shalako ceremony and feast has been closed to non-native peoples since 1990, and outsiders may only attend if invited by a Zuni tribal member.
